arrival_context: Google search for 'marriage licence' during early research, about 14 months out, no destination chosen yet.

first_impression.reaction: Sophie here. It answered the question in the first sentence: there's no licence in Australia, it's a notice to the celebrant, 1 to 18 months out. No 'dream day' waffle, linked straight to the Attorney-General's Department. As a lawyer I appreciate that. The 'not legal advice' line is the right call. The bit I actually care about, which country makes it legal, only really lands in the key takeaways, so I'd skim straight there and then jump to the overseas section.

journey.quote: If you are searching for a marriage licence in Australia, there is none to apply for.
journey.reaction: Straight answer, no throat clearing. This earns the skim.

journey.quote: The decision that shapes everything else is which country makes your marriage legal: Australia, with a symbolic ceremony abroad, or your destination, under its own law.
journey.reaction: This is the line I'd screenshot for James. It's the actual decision we haven't made yet. I wish it was in the intro rather than the fourth bullet.

journey.quote: The practical lesson: lodge the notice once your date and celebrant are settled, rather than in the final month.
"I call upon the persons here present to witness that I, A.B. (or C.D.), take thee, C.D. (or A.B.), to be my lawful wedded wife (or husband, or spouse)", or words to that effect.
journey.reaction: Accurate, and I don't mind reading statute, but this is where James would stop scrolling. It's celebrant territory, not ours. I skimmed past it.

journey.section: The certificates signed on the day
journey.quote: It is the one couples frame, but the commemorative certificate from your wedding day is not the official, legal marriage certificate.
journey.reaction: Didn't know that. Exactly the kind of thing that bites you later when you try to change your name. Trust up.

journey.quote: Couples from outside New Zealand sign a declaration at a registry office after they arrive, separate from the ceremony, and can only marry at the places named on the application, so name a wet weather alternative too.
journey.reaction: The wet weather tip is insider detail. That's the sort of thing that makes me think someone has actually done this, not just read a government page.

journey.quote: You apply online, then appear together in person before an agent no sooner than 30 days before the ceremony, each with valid government-issued photo ID.
journey.reaction: Clear. It also tells me marrying legally there means admin in the week we're supposed to be hosting 80 people, which the page doesn't quite spell out as a trade-off.

journey.quote: Some states and territories do not accept overseas marriage certificates for a name change, and in NSW you apply for an official change of name instead, which does not mean the marriage is unrecognised.
journey.reaction: We're in Sydney, so this matters. Honest, and it saves me a nasty surprise.

journey.section: Marry at home and celebrate abroad
journey.quote: The paperwork stays with you, your celebrant and the registry, while a Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments anywhere in the world, as your single point of contact from start to finish.
journey.reaction: Good that it's upfront the Advisor isn't doing the legal bit. But 'single point of contact from start to finish' is what every planner says. What does it actually mean for us: do they deal with our guests' travel, or just ours? Are the vendors their own people or whoever's local? 'Anywhere in the world' sounds a bit broad to believe.

journey.section: Plan your wedding abroad with Wedded Concierge
journey.quote: Whichever country makes it legal, one Wedded Advisor works in your time zone and quotes in AUD, and the fee is agreed in writing before any work begins.
journey.reaction: This is the best sales line on the page for me. AUD quotes and a fee in writing before anything starts goes straight at my worry about currency surprises and hidden costs. Still no idea what the fee roughly is, though.

journey.section: Plan your wedding abroad with Wedded Concierge
journey.quote: Tell us your date, your guest list and where you would like to marry, and begin with Wedded Concierge.
journey.reaction: We don't know where yet. That's the whole reason we're reading. It makes the enquiry feel like it's for people further along than us.

unanswered_questions: Roughly what does Wedded Concierge cost? Even a range or how the fee is worked out.
What does 'single point of contact from start to finish' include in practice? Does it cover guest travel and transfers for 60 to 90 people, half flying in internationally?
Are the vendors the Advisor uses their own vetted people, or are they found locally each time?
If we marry legally in Australia first, how close to the overseas celebration should we do it, and does the Advisor plan around that timing?
Is there a real wedding (venue and date) of a couple who did the symbolic ceremony route, so we can see what it looked like?
Can we enquire before we've chosen a destination, and what happens on that first call?

turn_offs_found.quote: a Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments anywhere in the world, as your single point of contact from start to finish.
turn_offs_found.why: Generic end-to-end claim with nothing specific behind it. 'Anywhere in the world' reads as a stretch.

would_share_with: James (partner): the key takeaways and the 'Choosing where to marry legally' section
Mum and Dad: the bit about the ceremonial certificate not being the legal one, since they'll ask

cta_reaction.quote: Whichever country makes it legal, one Wedded Advisor works in your time zone and quotes in AUD, and the fee is agreed in writing before any work begins.
cta_reaction.why: I'd click through to look at the Concierge page, but I wouldn't enquire off this post alone. It's a legal explainer and it's a good one, but I'd want two or three more posts and one real wedding first. The AUD and written fee line helps. The 'tell us where you would like to marry' wording assumes we already know.

top_3_changes: Put the real decision (which country makes the marriage legal) into the intro so skimmers like us hit it in the first lines, not the fourth takeaway.
State the trade-off of marrying legally in the destination plainly: the in-person steps described for New Zealand and Hawaii happen during the trip itself.
Let couples who haven't chosen a destination know they can still enquire, so the closing CTA doesn't feel like it's only for people further along.

suggested_edits.old: Marry abroad and the destination's law takes over, and some places do issue licences. This is general information as at November 2026, not legal advice.
suggested_edits.new: Marry abroad and the destination's law takes over, and some places do issue licences, so the first decision is which country makes your marriage legal. This is general information as at November 2026, not legal advice.
suggested_edits.why: Surfaces the decision we actually care about in the intro. Uses only wording already in the draft's key takeaways.

suggested_edits.old: The other path is to marry under the destination's law, as in New Zealand or Hawaii, so the ceremony your guests see is the legal one.
suggested_edits.new: The other path is to marry under the destination's law, as in New Zealand or Hawaii, so the ceremony your guests see is the legal one. The trade-off is that you follow the destination's own steps and timing, such as the in-person registry declaration in New Zealand or appearing before an agent in Hawaii, described above.
suggested_edits.why: Honest trade-off is a trust signal for us. Only restates steps already given in the New Zealand and Hawaii sections.

suggested_edits.old: Tell us your date, your guest list and where you would like to marry, and begin with
suggested_edits.new: Tell us your date, your guest list and where you would like to marry, or that you are still deciding, and begin with
suggested_edits.why: We're 14 months out with no destination. This makes the enquiry feel open to us without adding any claim about the service.
